What this data is

A survey of what people bought in the last two weeks, and what they do with it

  • BCE surveyed 10,289 people in France and Germany. Each respondent had bought running or sport-inspired footwear and described up to three purchases. Questions covered the brand and model, retailer or website, price, use, and other brands considered.
  • By surveying buyers directly, the report measures who buys each brand, where and why they buy it, and how they use the shoes. Point-of-sale data records the transaction; this report adds information about the buyer’s behavior and attitudes.
  • Figures are consumer-reported and unweighted. Unless otherwise stated, percentages represent shares of purchases within the selected group.
  • About this demo edition. Brands appear as Brand A to Brand M, retailers as Retailer 1 onward, and model families as Model A1 and so on. Bars and cells are drawn from illustrative placeholder data, and every figure label is masked as XX, so nothing on the page is a survey result. Written findings and implications are replaced by a note on what the licensed edition contains.

Questions this report answers

Point-of-sale data can tell you what sold. This report describes the person who bought it: what they bought, what they use it for, what they paid, and which brands they considered before choosing. Each question below links to the exhibit that answers it.

If you're a brand

Nine questions

  • Is my brand winning the buyer I think it is?→
  • Are buyers using my running shoes for running or for other activities?→
  • Are the youngest buyers choosing my brand?→
  • Does my brand perform better with men or with women?→
  • What motivates buyers to choose my brand?→
  • Does my brand win the serious runner or the occasional one?→
  • Is my brand holding its price?→
  • How many of my buyers are already shopping another brand?→
  • Is my brand in the doors where my buyers shop?→
If you're a retailer

Four questions

  • Which brands perform best at my business and at competing retailers?→
  • Is my footwear wall built for the buyer who walks in?→
  • Is demand moving toward my banner or away from it?→
  • Can one strategy cover France and Germany?→
Executive summary|By the numbersCountry-filtered

Headline figures for the market you select

The report treats the running category as two markets: the shoes that are run in, and the running shoes bought for everyday wear. The headline figures update when you select a country. Every number in the report is a share of purchases unless the chart says otherwise, and the base is shown on each chart. "All run" includes purchases identified by buyers as running shoes. "Run, used for run" and "Run, not used for run" divide those purchases by whether the shoes are mainly used for running or for other activities.

How each brand indexes with buyers aged 14 to 24

Buyers aged 14 to 24: how each brand's share among them compares with its share among all buyers
Each brand’s share among buyers aged 14 to 24 compared with its share among all buyers in the same cut, as an index where 100 means the two shares are equal. Rows are sorted by the 14 to 24 share.

Every brand on every measure, indexed to the market

One row per brand, each measure shown as an index against the market at 100. A green bar to the right means the brand is above the market on that measure, a red bar to the left means below it; discounting is reversed so that less discounting reads green. “All measures” shows every column at once; clicking a cell shows the percentages behind it, column headings sort, and “Show as” switches the table to percentages.

How each brand's share holds up, measure by measure
Each brand’s figure on the selected measure compared with the market, as an index where 100 means equal to the market. Made for run and Used for run compare the brand’s share of running-category purchases, and of purchases that are run in, with its share of all footwear; a brand’s green bars there mean a larger share of its purchases are running shoes, and are run in, than of purchases overall, not that it sells many pairs. Discounted 25%+ and Loyal to the same brand compare the brand’s rate with the market’s. Buyers 14 to 24, Women, Men, and €90 and over compare the brand’s share in that group with its share among all buyers.

Methodology
Demo edition. This page shows how the licensed report works. Brands, retailers, and model families are placeholders, and every figure on the page is illustrative, generated to exercise the exhibits; none is a survey result. The licensed edition carries the real brands, doors, figures, and BCE's written findings and implications.
France and Germany are two of the larger footwear markets in Western Europe. Both countries were surveyed using the same questionnaire, supporting consistent comparisons between them. The analysis covers 10,289 buyers and 17,533 purchases made in 2026.
BCE Consulting · Consumer Intelligence. Figures from the BCE France and Germany footwear survey, 2026: an online survey of 10,289 recent buyers (France 5,284, Germany 5,005) screened for a running or sport-inspired purchase in the prior 14 days, up to three purchases each, 17,533 branded purchases in all, consumer-reported and unweighted. Seventy-eight respondents whose answers matched a duplicated-profile pattern were removed before analysis. Price is estimated by blending the price bands and the exact euro amounts buyers reported.
Charts marked “segment-filtered” or “country-filtered” carry their own toggle and show the active cut and base. First edition of a continuous tracking survey; no annualized or year-over-year figures. Awareness not surveyed. Market sizing out of scope for this edition.

About this report. The BCE France and Germany Running & Sportstyle Report is a consumer purchase study designed and fielded by BCE Consulting with Qualtrics, covering 10,289 buyers and 17,533 footwear purchases.
